intro: To write a nursing care plan with a NANDA diagnosis, state the problem, the related factor, and the defining characteristics in one statement. Then confirm the label in the NANDA-I source your facility uses, and keep patient details out of anything you draft with AI.
tldr: A NANDA-I diagnosis is a short label plus a related factor and the signs that support it. Write it from your own assessment, not from a list.
The time cost is real, but the best numbers measure charting in general, not care plans specifically.
Build one blank template with no patient details, dictate the first draft, then edit it against the chart.
Check your employer's rules before you paste any patient information into an AI tool, Lazur included.

blocks.text: The care plan usually gets written when the shift is almost over. You have already charted vitals, medications, and many small findings. Now the plan asks for a label, a cause, a goal, and a review date. That is a different kind of thinking, and it is where most of the time goes. The good news is that the work follows a pattern you can learn quickly.
NANDA-I nursing diagnosis format: related factor and defining characteristics

A NANDA-I diagnosis is a standardized nursing label. Many nurses write it in three parts: the problem, the related factor, and the defining characteristics. You may see this shorthand called PES, for problem, etiology, and signs and symptoms. The problem is the label. The related factor is the cause or contributing condition you can act on. The defining characteristics are the observations that support the label.

Here is an example. A patient recovering from surgery cannot turn in bed without help. You see reddened skin over the sacrum that stays red after pressure is relieved. The candidate label is impaired skin integrity. The related factor is immobility. The defining characteristics are the redness and the need for help to reposition. Written out, the statement reads: impaired skin integrity related to immobility as evidenced by persistent redness over the sacrum and need for help with repositioning.
Step by step: from assessment to a finished care plan

items: Start from what you assessed. Write the finding in plain words before you think about a label.
Pick one or two candidate labels that match the finding. Do not pick more than you can support.
Confirm each label in the approved NANDA-I source your facility uses. Copy the exact wording when your policy requires it.
Write the related factor as one cause you can act on, such as immobility or a new medication effect.
Write the defining characteristics as observations from this shift, with times if your unit asks for them.
Set one measurable goal and two or three interventions tied to the related factor. Name who does each one.
Schedule a reassessment and write the date into the plan. A plan with no review date goes stale fast.

blocks.text: Most patients have only a few active nursing diagnoses at one time. If your list runs long, rank the ones that change care this shift. Put those first. Leave the rest for the next review, so the plan stays readable at handoff.
NANDA care plan examples by finding

rows: Reddened skin over the sacrum that stays red after pressure is relieved
Needs help to stand and sways when walking
Weakness, new medication effect, or unfamiliar surroundings
Reports pain and guards the incision when moving
blocks.caption: Examples only. Confirm every label in your approved source before you use it.

blocks.text: Worked example: updating a carried-forward plan

Suppose you open yesterday's plan for a patient who now walks the hall with one person helping. The old label still reads impaired physical mobility. Today's assessment shows several walks a shift, with steady gait and help only at the door. Update the label, the related factor, and the signs before you touch the goal. A goal that still says bed mobility makes the plan look current when it is not.
Nursing documentation time: what the studies measured
Most of the time figures in the research describe charting in general, not care plans. Use them to size the problem. Do not use them to predict your own shift.

The strongest time figure comes from one academic health system. Vendor log data put flowsheet charting at a mean of 31.11% of a 12-hour shift in February 2023. Nurses in focus groups in the same study estimated that 10% to 50% of the shift goes to EHR documentation, and many saw that as appropriate. Self-estimates and log data measure different things, so do not combine them.

The KLAS survey points toward retention. As HealthSystemCIO summarizes it, 46% of critical-care nurses lose 3 or more hours a week to unproductive charting. Nurses who lose that much time report 46% burnout and 34% likely to leave. Nurses who lose under 1 hour report 21% burnout and 20% turnover risk. The same summary says 40% of nurses intend to leave the profession by 2029. The original KLAS report was not reviewed for this page, so treat these as the summary's figures.

The only study here that measured a fix comes from German long-term care. Voice documentation cut mean morning-shift documentation from 53.91 minutes to 39.10 minutes, an adjusted cut of 15 minutes. It was a single-group study across 14 facilities. It did not report care plans separately, so use it as a hint about voice tools, not a promise for your unit.
Mistakes people make with NANDA care plans

items: Choosing the label that sounds most serious instead of the one the signs support.
Writing defining characteristics from memory after the shift ends.
Listing every problem you saw, which buries the one the team needs to act on.
Writing a goal as a task, such as turn patient, instead of an observable change.
Pasting full taxonomy definitions into shared documents without checking your license.
Leaving out a reassessment date, so the plan never gets reviewed.

blocks.text: Edge cases: risk labels, unlisted problems, and disagreements

Risk labels work differently. A risk diagnosis describes a problem that has not happened yet, so it lists risk factors instead of defining characteristics. Mixing the two is a common error. Check the source for the exact structure before you write a risk label into a plan.

When no label fits, do not force one. Write the finding in plain words. Then raise it with your educator or charge nurse. The unit may have an approved option, or the situation may call for a different kind of plan. Document what you saw, and hold the label until you confirm it.

When a colleague's label differs from yours, compare the signs first. If the signs match, the difference is probably wording. If the signs differ, look at the chart together before you change anyone's plan. Honest readings of the same chart can still need a conversation.
Nursing care plan template on Mac without copied NANDA text

A template saves time only if it holds your structure, not someone else's text. Build the headings yourself: problem, related factor, defining characteristics, goal, interventions, and reassessment. Keep the label list in your approved source, and let the template hold your wording.

In Apple Pages, choose File > New to start from a template. To always open one template, go to Pages > Settings > General and set 'Use template'. Hold Option and choose File > New from Template Chooser to pick a different template for one document. Apple's guide does not show how to save a custom template, so check Apple's custom template article before you build one.
Word works in a similar way. This page does not list Word menu steps, so check Microsoft's help for your version. For layout ideas, read [Word for nurses on Mac](/for/nurses/word).
Privacy and licensing before any AI tool touches your draft

Patient information stays under your employer's rules. Before you hold any shortcut over a chart, ask whether an AI tool is allowed on that screen. Policies differ between employers, so do not assume that what worked at a past job still applies.

Lazur sees your screen only while you hold ⌥ ⌘. Your audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those are the product's stated terms, not a legal review. Your facility decides what is allowed on the unit.
Work from a de-identified case while you learn. Put patient details only into systems your employer approves. If you are unsure, ask your privacy officer before you try a new tool on a live chart.

faq.question: Do I have to use NANDA-I labels in my care plan?
faq.answer: It depends on your employer. Some facilities require NANDA-I labels, and others use their own care plan modules. Ask your unit educator which system applies to you, then use the approved list and its wording.

faq.question: Can I copy NANDA-I definitions into my own template?
faq.answer: Not freely. NANDA International says unauthorized use, reproduction, or distribution of its classification is prohibited. Keep label names and your own wording in the template, and check your facility's license before you share anything.

faq.question: How do I get NANDA-I labels without buying the book?
faq.answer: NANDA International lists three routes: the published book, INKA memberships, and NANDA 360 pages. An institution may already pay for one of them, so ask your library before you buy anything.

faq.question: Can Lazur write my nursing care plan?
faq.answer: Lazur can explain the parts, point at fields, guide you through a screen, dictate text, and draft a template for you to check. It does not know your patient unless you describe the case. It does not replace your assessment or your facility's approved source.

faq.question: Is it safe to use Lazur near a patient chart?
faq.answer: Lazur looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. The audio and screenshot go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Your employer's rules still apply, so do not hold the shortcut over a chart unless your policy allows it.

faq.question: What if the label I need is not in the list?
faq.answer: Use the closest approved label and write the gap in your own words. Ask your educator whether the situation needs a different kind of plan. Do not invent a label that only sounds official.

faq.question: Does a nursing diagnosis replace a medical diagnosis?
faq.answer: No. A nursing diagnosis describes a response to a health problem that nursing care can address. A medical diagnosis names a disease or condition. Both can appear in the same chart, and each does a different job.

faq.question: Where do the time figures on this page come from?
faq.answer: The 31.11% figure comes from vendor log data at one academic health system in February 2023. The 46% and 34% figures come from a KLAS survey as summarized by HealthSystemCIO. The 15 minutes figure comes from a German long-term care study that did not cover care plans.

costs.title: Shift time you do not get back
costs.text: Charting takes the part of the shift that should go to patients. One academic health system's vendor logs put flowsheet charting at a mean of 31.11% of a 12-hour shift in February 2023. That study measured flowsheets, not care plans, but care plans live in the same charting workflow.

costs.title: Burnout and retention
costs.text: KLAS survey data, as summarized by HealthSystemCIO, links unproductive charting to how nurses feel about the job. Nurses who lose 3 or more hours a week report 46% burnout, against 21% for those who lose under 1 hour. These are associations. They do not prove that care plans cause burnout.

costs.title: Patient data and licensing risk
costs.text: Pasting patient details into an AI tool can break your employer's rules. NANDA International says unauthorized use, reproduction, or distribution of its classification is prohibited. A template full of copied definitions can cross that line without anyone noticing.

costs.title: Diagnosis errors you cannot yet measure
costs.text: No source reviewed for this page measures harm from drafting errors, so this page gives no rate. The risk is still concrete. A label that does not match the assessment points the team at the wrong problem. Treat every label as a claim you must support with what you saw.

causes.title: Flowsheets multiply entries
causes.text: Structured charting produces a lot of entries. Prior work cited in the JMIR Nursing study reports 631 to 875 flowsheet entries per 12-hour shift, about one per minute. A care plan built from flowsheet data inherits that volume. Copying values forward can make it look complete while it stays thin.

causes.title: Diagnosis wording takes practice
causes.text: Writing a good diagnosis statement is a skill that improves with repetition. Without a fixed reference open at the desk, each nurse invents phrasing, and the team cannot compare notes. The classification is reached through the published book, INKA memberships, or NANDA 360 pages, so the source is not always within reach.

causes.title: Old plans get copied forward
causes.text: A saved care plan from last week is faster than a blank page. The trouble starts when the patient changed but the label, factor, and goal did not. Carry-forward errors look like good documentation until a new nurse or reviewer reads them closely.

causes.title: Charting happens after the work
causes.text: Many plans get written at the end of the shift, from memory. Details drift. The defining characteristics you write may describe an earlier part of the day. Writing the plan during the shift keeps the signs accurate and the time short.

causes.title: Templates that do not fit the unit
causes.text: Some electronic records offer fixed care plan modules. If the module does not match how your unit works, you type around it. That extra typing is the time cost you feel most.

fixes.title: Write from the assessment first
fixes.text: Start with what you measured. Write the finding in plain words, such as reddened skin over the tailbone that stays red, or a patient who cannot turn without help. Then ask which label fits. Starting from the label list invites a term that sounds right but does not match the chart.

fixes.title: Use the three-part statement
fixes.text: Write the label, then related to, then as evidenced by. For example: impaired skin integrity related to immobility as evidenced by persistent redness over the sacrum. Keep the related factor to one cause you can act on. Keep the signs to what you observed on this shift.

fixes.title: Check the label in a source you can reach
fixes.text: Use the NANDA-I source your facility licenses. That may be a library copy of the book, an INKA membership, or NANDA 360 access through an institution. If you have none, ask your unit educator for the approved list. Online lists disagree on basic counts, so they make weak references.

fixes.title: Build one blank template
fixes.text: Make one document with headings and no patient names. Use problem, related factor, defining characteristics, goal, interventions, and reassessment. In Apple Pages, start from File > New. Set Pages > Settings > General > 'Use template' if you want one template to open by default. Keep label names and your own wording in the boxes.

fixes.title: Dictate the first draft, then edit
fixes.text: Hold fn and speak the draft in plain words. Dictation types clean text at the cursor in any app. Then read the draft aloud and fix the label, factor, and signs before the goal. Dictation saves typing, not judgment, so the edit pass still matters.

fixes.title: Set fixed charting moments each shift
fixes.text: Pick one time mid-shift and one before handoff for care plans. Set a Reminders alert or a timer for each. Fixed moments beat charting whenever you happen to remember. This only helps if you check each diagnosis against the chart at those times.

fixes.title: Practice on one anonymized case with a peer
fixes.text: Pick one case from your unit with every identifier removed. Draft the plan, then compare labels with a preceptor or charge nurse. Write down each disagreement and the reason. Keep that list, and reuse it on the next case.

fixes.title: Mark what you have not verified
fixes.text: When a label, number, or source is uncertain, write it as unverified in your own notes. Then check it before it becomes a phrase the whole unit copies. This habit keeps guesses out of shared templates.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Pick one practice case
plan.text: Choose one anonymized case from your unit. Remove names, dates, room numbers, and every other identifier. Write the finding in plain words only. Do not use real chart data in any AI tool.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Check the label
plan.text: Find each candidate label in your approved NANDA-I source. Write the exact wording in your own notes. Record which source you used and how you reached it.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Build the template
plan.text: Make one blank Word or Pages document with six headings: problem, related factor, defining characteristics, goal, interventions, and reassessment. Keep it free of patient data. Save a copy you can reuse.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Dictate and edit
plan.text: Hold fn and dictate the case draft in plain words. Read it aloud. Fix the label, the related factor, and the signs first. Then tighten the goal and the interventions.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Review with a peer
plan.text: Share the draft with a preceptor or charge nurse. Ask one question: do the signs support the label? Write down what changed and why. Add the useful phrases to your notes.

plan.label: Every shift
plan.title: Write during the shift
plan.text: Write or update the plan during the shift, not after it. Set one reminder before handoff to check each diagnosis against the chart. Mark any label you could not verify.
